title: DNS Whispers
description: Our IDS flagged a workstation making a lot of odd DNS lookups to a domain nobody recognizes. No file ever left over HTTP... but data left anyway.

title: Picture Perfect
description: Someone sent us this souvenir picture from the Axios office. The image itself is boring. The *file*, on the other hand, remembers where it's been.

title: Ghost in Binary
description:
Months ago, an unknown program slipped through a company's internal network. It stole nothing and encrypted nothing. Then it vanished from every machine it touched.
All the responders kept is a single fingerprint of the sample, code-named Agent. The author left no signature, no taunt and no confession. Analysts believe the only words this file will ever say are the ones it says when it's out of its depth.
Find the sample and listen closely to how it begins.
SHA-256: 881941ea24e92f4bd4d69d79e27ce1d2b10094172cb3cc93b223daf70ef2d867
Flag format: BreachPoint{Your_Found_Text_With_Underscores}

title: Locked Room
description:
We seized a device and pulled everything off it. The secret is right there in the
evidence — sealed inside an encrypted vault. The catch: the person who sealed it
used a device that throws the key away the instant the v      ault closes.

title: Whisper
description:
We intercepted a short message, but it was "encrypted" by someone who thought
one byte of key was enough to keep a secret. It wasn't.

title: Nonce Vault
description:
We recovered a capture from a logging service that encrypts every line with
**AES-256-CTR**. Helpfully, for most lines we have both the plaintext and the
ciphertext. For one line — the interesting one — we only have the ciphertext.

Stream ciphers are famously fragile when people get lazy with nonces...

title: Mixed Signals
description:
At 03:12 a.m., the HALCYON-7 escrow appliance at Meridian Custody locked itself in the middle of a release ceremony. The tamper circuit wiped the key store before anyone could react, but our incident team managed to pull a raw capture off the diagnostics bridge in the seconds before it went dark.
The bridge was built for field technicians debugging failed key ceremonies. It shows a small window of each secret prime: the top bits of one of them in raw binary, and, because the front-panel LCD only speaks decimal, the last digits of the other.
The vendor's incident statement is confident:
"A couple of fragments cannot reconstruct a 1024-bit key. No customer data was exposed."
Their statement is half right: neither fragment is enough by itself. The escrow release token is still sitting in the capture, sealed under a key that no longer exists anywhere except in the maths.
Recover the token.
Files
Capture.bin -> Raw diagnostics-bridge capture from the incident
Vault_fw.py -> Firmware excerpt: framing, leak logic, key derivation, sealing (secrets stripped)

Title: twin primes
description:
Our intern generated an RSA key pair in a hurry. "1024 bits, that's plenty," they
said, and picked the two primes... one right after the other.

title: Cookie Quest
description:
The Axios "Members Area" remembers who you are with a session cookie. Regular
members can't see the internal flag — only admins can. Become one.

title: Postcard
description: Axios Postcards renders your message **on the server** so it always looks perfect. Maybe it renders it a little too literally.

title: Notary JWT
description:
The Axios Notary hands every visitor a signed JWT. Guests get `role: guest`;
only `role: admin` may read `/flag`. In the spirit of openness, the signing key's
**public half is published** at `/pubkey` and `/.well-known/jwks.json`. Inspect
everything. Forge yourself an admin token.

title: Ret2Win
description:
There's a `win()` function in this binary that never gets called. It prints the flag — but only if you call it *with the right argument*.

Connect: nc 34.42.168.21 5002

title: Fortified
description:
Yes, there's a buffer overflow. There's also a stack canary, PIE, full RELRO, NX, and not a single byte of output you can turn into a leak. The `print_flag()` function exists — it's just never called, and you have no way to find it.
 Connect: nc 34.42.168.21 5003

title: Neighbors
description:
The security console asks for your name and stores it right next to a flag that says whether you're authorized. What could go wrong?

Connect: nc 34.42.168.21 5001

Title: xor license
description:
We found this license checker. Supposedly, the *only* key it accepts is also the
flag. Feed it the right string and it will tell you.

Title: oneway
description:
We intercepted a short message, but it was "encrypted" by someone who thought
one byte of key was enough to keep a secret. It wasn't.

Title: layercake
Description:
One layer of obfuscation is a speed bump. This checker has four, stacked on top
of each other, and it will only say "Correct!" for exactly one input.
